text: The project is a software system and needs no special electronic hardware. The prototype was developed and tested on an ordinary laptop. The server for the cloud deployment is a small virtual machine.

caption: Table 4.1: Hardware used
rows: Laptop with the Windows 11 operating system
Any computer or phone with a current web browser (Chrome was used for testing)
Hardhat local Ethereum node running on the development laptop
Oracle Cloud free-tier virtual machine (x86-64, 1 GB of memory, 44 GB disk) running Ubuntu 24.04 and Docker, with ports 80 and 443 open and 2 GB of swap space added
Three separate computers or accounts, each holding one encrypted key share

caption: Table 4.2: Software used
rows: Runtime for the backend, scripts and tests
Database for the roll and token hashes
Talking to the blockchain from the backend and tools
Splitting and rebuilding the election key
Security headers and the content security policy
Container image and the two-container setup
Virtual machine to host the server
Free public domain name for the server
Public Proof-of-Stake Ethereum test network (chain id 11155111), viewed through Etherscan

text: The system was developed in stages, and each stage was tested before the next began: first the smart contract and its tests; then the key ceremony; then the backend with the voter hash and the token logic; then the voting and administrator pages; then the one-button demonstration page; and last the deployment tooling for Sepolia and the cloud server. The code was organised as follows.

caption: Table 4.3: Organisation of the project code
rows: Express server, voter hash, token store, blockchain client, one-button mode
Voting and administrator pages and the ballot encryption
Key ceremony, administrator commands, tally, submit-tally, verify-tally, deployment, bundle and demo launcher
Container image, two-container setup and HTTPS proxy
Contract tests, backend and cryptography tests, deployment tests

text: Two practical problems found during development affected correctness. First, sending two transactions quickly one after the other made the library reuse a transaction number, so the second failed; the fix was to turn off the library's short-term cache of the account's transaction count. Second, on a fresh local chain the clock of the chain lagged behind real time, so the contract answered that voting was not yet open; the start-up script now mines a block and uses the chain's own time.
